methods.label: Construct infinitely many valid pairs
methods.explanation:
To prove that the number of pairs is not finite, it is enough to produce infinitely many distinct positive-integer solutions. Rearranging and factoring gives
\[
y^2=x^3-x^2=x^2(x-1).
\]
The factor \(x^2\) is already a square, so we can make the right side a square by choosing \(x-1\) to be a square as well.

For any positive integer \(n\), take
\[
x=n^2+1,
\qquad
y=n(n^2+1)=nx.
\]
Both numbers are positive integers. Substitution verifies the original equation:
\[
x^2+y^2=x^2+n^2x^2
=x^2(1+n^2)=x^3.
\]
As \(n\) increases through the positive integers, \(x=n^2+1\) strictly increases, so no two constructed pairs are the same. There are therefore \(\boxed{\text{infinitely many}}\) pairs, choice \(\mathrm{D}\).
methods.levelReason: Elementary factorization reveals an indexed family of integer solutions; direct verification and distinctness prove infinitude.
